g11-geography-ug4-t1.overview: The Growth of World Population sits inside Global Population Dynamics and Challenges. Population growth is the focus of Unit 4 of Grade 11 Geography in the Ethiopian (FDRE Ministry of Education) curriculum. First, it follows the world’s population from one billion in 1800 toward almost eleven billion by 2100, using the demographic transition model. Then it contrasts fast-growing less developed countries with the ageing, slow-growing developed world, and it turns to migration and to the policies that steer population growth, linking on to Unit 5: Geography and Economic Development. Students will also learn how population growth applies to real-life situations.
objectives: Trace the trend of world population growth from 1800 to 2100.
Compare population trends in less developed and more developed countries.
Explain the main factors behind accelerated growth.
Calculate fertility, mortality, and migration measures from given data.
Distinguish free migration from forced migration and name key sender and receiver countries.
g11-geography-ug4-t1.simple:
The Growth of World Population in plain words. The exam wants you to recognise the core ideas, not to memorise whole paragraphs. Focus on:
  • First, the five stages of the demographic transition, from high birth and death rates to low ones.
  • How falling fertility and mortality reshaped the world since 1800.
  • Then the rapid rise of less developed countries and the slow, ageing growth of developed ones.
  • Finally, adolescent fertility, the demographic dividend, and the support-ratio squeeze.
g11-geography-ug4-t1.detailed:
The Growth of World Population — the essentials. First, the five stages of the demographic transition, from high birth and death rates to low ones. How falling fertility and mortality reshaped the world since 1800. Then the rapid rise of less developed countries and the slow, ageing growth of developed ones. Finally, adolescent fertility, the demographic dividend, and the support-ratio squeeze.

What the MoE expects you to be able to do:

  • Trace the trend of world population growth from 1800 to 2100.
  • Compare population trends in less developed and more developed countries.
  • Explain the main factors behind accelerated growth.
  • Calculate fertility, mortality, and migration measures from given data.
  • Distinguish free migration from forced migration and name key sender and receiver countries.
